https://www.politico.eu/article/europe-d.text: PARIS — Governments should change laws to allow defense companies to take down suspicious drones overflying their plants, said a senior executive at Franco-German arms-maker KNDS. The call, which KNDS plans to take to Brussels, comes amid a wave of fires, sabotage attempts and espionage cases targeting European weapons manufacturers — several of which capitals have linked to Russia. “It would be good if national legislation allowed defense companies to protect themselves against drones — especially first-person-view drones that pass through layered air defense,” KNDS Executive Vice President for International Development Marcel Grisnigt said in an interview. Advertisement Advertisement Currently, “the only thing we can do is warn local authorities and ask them to take measures. Most of the time, it’s too late obviously, and the harm has already been done,” he added. “We are developing and producing countermeasures ourselves. They could be deployed to protect our own sites, but then you need to have the legal authorization.” Such systems can either cut off a drone's connection to an operator, forcing it to land or fly off, or physically knock it out of the sky. In many European countries, only law enforcement and the armed forces are allowed to operate counter-drone systems — not companies. Leaders, including French President Emmanuel Macron and Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk, have warned that countries should brace for increased threats from Moscow as the Kremlin escalates pressure on Ukraine’s allies. French President Emmanuel Macron greets Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk in Paris on July 13, 2026. | Pool photo by Teresa Suarez via AFP/Getty Images Last week, Estonia accused Russian intelligence of being behind an August arson attack on arms contractor Milrem Robotics. Poland, Germany, Slovakia, Italy, Bulgaria and others are also investigating suspicious incidents at arms plants — many used to supply Ukraine with weapons and ammunition. "Arms factories in European countries that produce weapons for Ukraine are potential military targets for Russia," said Russian foreign ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova on Wednesday. “It should not be assumed that military facilities outside Ukrainian territory that produce weapons for the Kyiv regime will be safe. Anyone who thinks so is mistaken.” No 'luxury of time' The EU and NATO are reacting, but Grisnigt warned this will take time. Advertisement Advertisement European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has pitched a new EU mechanism to counter hybrid threats, while NATO’s top military commander, U.S. Gen. Alexus Grynkewich, called on allied countries to share more intelligence on Russian hybrid attacks. “We hear more and more calls for NATO’s Article 4 [which enables consultation after a threat] and a push for countries to align. OK, but how much time is this going to take? We do not have the luxury of time,” Grisnigt said. “We are ramping up enormously toward Europe’s readiness in 2030, but if defense capacity is interrupted by hybrid warfare, then we won’t be ready in 2030.” KNDS, which makes the German Leopard 2 tank and the French Caesar self-propelled howitzer, has faced its own suspicious incidents and beefed up staffing and security measures. A soldier carries ammunition to load a Caesar Mk-I wheeled self-propelled howitzer during an exercise by Lithuanian and French troops along with NATO allies in Pabradė, Lithuania on Sept. 16, 2026. | Petras Malukas/AFP via Getty Images In July, a Moldovan man was arrested on suspicion of espionage after flying a drone over a KNDS factory in Munich. In France, fires at power installations supplying KNDS France and missile-maker MBDA plants are being treated by the Paris Public Prosecutor's Office as a possible “violation of the nation's fundamental interests.” The KNDS executive praised the French model: Under the military planning law formally adopted over the summer, French weapons manufacturers and operators of critical infrastructure, such as telecom and transport companies, are allowed to use counter-drone systems on their sites themselves. German legislation, Grisnigt complained, does not allow defense companies to do the same. Advertisement Advertisement European coordination KNDS wants defense companies treated like critical infrastructure — and to benefit from the same protections. Under EU rules, operators of critical infrastructure — which include power grids, telecommunications networks and ports but not the defense industry — are required to meet security obligations. They also get support from public authorities, including threat information. “The first thing we would need is simply access to intelligence. Based on intelligence, you can act,” Grisnigt stressed. “Of course, protecting critical infrastructure is a national responsibility, but these kinds of threats are cross-border,” he added. “We need a strong European framework that would link national protection in a consistent approach.” KNDS wants the European Commission to “urgently create” a task force that would stress-test the defense industrial base against hybrid threats. The measures put in place to protect sites should be eligible for cash from the European Competitiveness Fund in the EU's next long-term budget, “so that you do not have only a national burden but a shared financial burden,” according to the executive. KNDS started approaching other European weapons makers and will address the issue with European Defense Commissioner Andrius Kubilius in the coming weeks. “Let's be honest ... If we are already not prepared to protect ourselves now, then we are neither prepared for the worst-case scenario," Grisnigt said. Advertisement Advertisement

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c8ly.text: Image source, Getty Images Image caption, There are currently 300,000 Agniveers serving in India's defence forces By Nikita Yadav BBC News, Delhi Published 16 November 2026 For generations of young Indians, joining the armed forces offered something few other jobs did - a steady career, financial security, the promise of a pension after retirement and the pride of serving their country. In 2022, the government upended that arrangement, announcing a new reform scheme under which young men and women entering the military would serve for just four years. Only a quarter would be allowed to stay on permanently. The rest would return to civilian life with a lump-sum payment, but without the pension and other benefits that had long made military service an attractive career. Now, as the first batch of recruits prepares to complete its four-year term, the government is offering them a chance to stay longer, in a significant shift in a policy that has been fiercely debated since its introduction. On 4 November, Chief of Defence Staff General NS Raja Subramani announced that recruits who failed to secure permanent positions under the Agnipath, or "path of fire", programme would be offered another two years of service at higher pay. They would then get a second opportunity to join the regular forces, provided they met the selection criteria. Gen Subramani said the decision followed feedback from the forces and insisted that Agnipath would continue. But the timing is significant. More than 18,300 recruits from the first batch are due to complete their initial tenure by the end of 2026. Officials say the new arrangement will be offered to more than 300,000 Agniveers - as recruits under the scheme are known - currently serving across the army, navy and air force. Whether future batches will also be covered remains unclear. The BBC has contacted the defence ministry for clarification. The ministry has defended , external Agnipath, saying internal assessments found the recruits to be physically fit, motivated and technologically adaptable. It also said the scheme had widened recruitment across districts and made the process more standardised. But the extension has brought renewed attention to the trade-offs at the heart of the policy - and whether its original ambitions were realistic. Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, Those selected are trained for months before being inducted into regiments When the government introduced Agnipath, it argued the scheme would reduce the average age of the armed forces, lower long-term salary and pension costs and create a younger, more technologically adaptable fighting force. But military experts and opposition leaders have questioned whether a four-year contract could replace what had traditionally been a coveted, long-term career in the armed forces. "Being a soldier in the armed forces was a chance for these young men to make a life for themselves, to get their families out of poor or lower-middle-income conditions," says retired Maj Gen Yash Mor, a vocal critic of the scheme. These concerns were also amplified by the timing of Agnipath's launch. Recruitment had been suspended for nearly two years during the Covid pandemic, leaving thousands of aspirants waiting for vacancies to reopen. The changes were greeted by massive protests across the country, with many saying the career path they had spent years preparing for had fundamentally changed. This sentiment was felt most in states and cities that have traditionally been major recruitment hubs, where military service has been a family tradition for generations. Kulbeer Singh Chaudhary, who runs a recruitment training institute in Dehradun city, says interest in joining the armed forces fell sharply and he stopped conducting Agniveer training batches. The latest announcement, he hopes, would reverse that trend. "The possibility of a longer engagement and eventual absorption into the forces may offer young candidates greater assurance," he says. The changes also come at a time when the armed forces are facing personnel shortages. In November last year, The Indian Express reported , external that the army alone faced a shortfall of nearly 180,000 soldiers and was considering increasing recruitment. Image source, Bloomberg via Getty Images Image caption, Many young men from small towns spend months preparing for the selection process to join the defence forces But the debate over Agnipath goes beyond what happens to recruits after four years. Critics also question whether that is enough time to turn them into experienced soldiers. Sanjiv Krishan Sood, a former additional director general of the Border Security Force, has argued , external that the shorter training period is particularly problematic for technical roles requiring specialised skills. Retired Maj Gen Mor says military effectiveness depends on experience and trust built over years. "It takes eight-to-nine years to turn a raw recruit into a dependable, seasoned soldier - someone capable of handling a tank crew, an artillery gun crew or a small detachment," he says. "Over those years, a soldier develops the ethos, camaraderie, brotherhood and fighting spirit that bind a unit together. These qualities cannot be built overnight." Sood says the additional two years could help improve recruits' skills, particularly in handling specialised equipment. Senior military leaders have also welcomed the extension. Air Vice Marshal Shekhar Yadav told news agency ANI , external it would allow the forces to retain trained personnel for longer. But the change could create fresh challenges within military units. Regular soldiers, Agniveers on four-year contracts and those serving an additional two years could find themselves working alongside one another despite differences in pay, promotion prospects and post-service benefits. Experts warn that these disparities could affect unit cohesion. Image source, NurPhoto via Getty Images Image caption, Indian soldiers are deployed through the year at the country's borders with China and Pakistan There is also the question of whether the changes will undermine one of the government's central objectives: reducing spending. Almost half of India's defence budget , external goes towards salaries and pensions, leaving less money for modernisation and new equipment. By limiting the number of personnel eligible for long-term benefits, Agnipath was expected to ease that burden. But critics argue that savings should not come at the expense of military effectiveness. "We are not against making changes, but there are ways and means to go about it," says Mor, adding that the government could instead reduce annual recruitment while retaining soldiers for longer periods. He also points to India's tense borders with Pakistan and China, where troops remain deployed year-round, placing sustained demands on manpower and operational experience. Retired Major-General Birender Singh Dhanoa, meanwhile, questions whether shorter service makes financial sense when the military is investing in training to operate increasingly sophisticated equipment. "The amount of time it takes to train, and the financial outlay for training, is much higher for modern equipment. So shouldn't you get the best bang for your buck?" he asks. Many retired officers had proposed a different approach when the scheme was announced, he says. "We suggested that if you want to reduce your financial burden, you increase the terms and conditions of service. Take these guys for eight-or-nine years and retain a larger number after that." The announcement also comes at a politically sensitive time. Elections are due soon in Punjab, Uttar Pradesh and Uttarakhand - states that have traditionally supplied large numbers of soldiers and where military recruitment remains an important source of employment. The opposition Congress party has called the revision a "u-turn", alleging that the government is responding to fears of losing votes. For young recruits approaching the end of their contracts, the changes offer some reassurance, but few guarantees. Two more years of service could mean more money, greater experience and another chance at a permanent career. But for many, it also means putting their futures on hold, without knowing whether they will eventually be allowed to stay. https://hotnews.ro/ministrul-german-al-a.text: Ministrul german al apărării, Boris Pistorius, a declarat vineri că şi-a cerut scuze pentru că a calificat drept „stupidă” opoziţia secretarului adjunct american al apărării Elbridge Colby faţă de loviturile ucrainene în profunzimea Rusiei, adăugând însă că nu-şi retrage criticile faţă de poziţia oficialului SUA, relatează Reuters, preluată de Agerpres. Schimbul tensionat de replici dintre cei doi oficiali a avut loc marţi la sediul NATO din Bruxelles şi a evidenţiat divergenţele dintre SUA şi susţinătorii europeni ai Ucrainei cu privire la strategia militară a acesteia din urmă de a aduce războiul pe teritoriul Rusiei prin atacuri continue cu drone în special asupra rafinăriilor, dar şi a altor obiective, precum infrastructuri portuare, companii ale complexului militar-industrial şi depozite ale companiilor de comerţ electronic. „Privind înapoi, cred acum că alegerea cuvintelor a fost nepotrivită ”, a declarat Pistorius pentru publicaţia Politico. El a susţinut că, nefiind vorbitor nativ de limba engleză, a folosit o formulare nefericită la o conferinţă de presă. „Nu ar fi trebuit să fac asta”, a continuat el, adăugând că i-a telefonat lui Colby miercuri pentru a discuta despre incident. „Mi-am cerut scuze pentru cuvintele folosite, dar am subliniat în acelaşi timp – şi el vede acest lucru la fel – că pur şi simplu avem puncte de vedere diferite asupra acestei chestiuni”, a mai spus ministrul german. Elbridge Colby, care este responsabil cu politica Pentagonului, criticase Ucraina pentru atacurile în profunzimea Rusiei, vorbind la o nouă reuniune a Grupului de contact pentru apărarea Ucrainei, cunoscut şi ca grupul de la Ramstein şi format din statele care sprijină militar Ucraina, unde s-a discutat despre sporirea livrărilor de armament către aceasta. Potrivit responsabilului american, aceste atacuri ucrainene nu ajută semnificativ la diminuarea potenţialului militar al Rusiei, în schimb riscă să sporească determinarea populaţiei ruse de a sprijini continuarea războiului împotriva Ucrainei. „Deşi dezbaterea publică se concentrează pe spectacolul loviturilor în profunzime menite să provoace suferinţă populaţiei ruse, evaluarea noastră este că astfel de lovituri nu au fost eficiente în a contribui la încheierea războiului şi nici nu contribuie la oprirea înaintării ruse pe linia frontului”, a avertizat Colby. Întrebat apoi, la o conferinţă de presă, dacă împărtăşeşte poziţia exprimată de adjunctul şefului Pentagonului, ministrul german al apărării a răspuns că „a critica loviturile care distrug în Rusia ţinte militare strategice sau folosite în scopuri militare (…) este un lucru destul de stupid”. Mai mult, ministrul Boris Pistorius a adăugat că „ar trebui mai degrabă să criticăm şi să vorbim despre atacurile teroriste care au loc zi şi noapte (…) asupra infrastructurii energetice, de apă şi de încălzire în Ucraina”. https://www.digi24.ro/stiri/actualitate/.text: Comisia de Etică a Universităţii din Craiova a publicat, vineri, raportul cu privire la suspiciunea de plagiat, invocată în două sesizări care au vizat lucrarea „Sistemul mijloacelor de probă în procesul civil” (2009), elaborată de Radu Marinescu. Concluzia comisiei este că „s-a constatat existenţa” plagiatului, dar concluziile celor 8 specialişti din dosar au fost „contradictorii şi interpretabile”. În consecinţă, Comisia a anunţat că a respins sesizările, însă decizia poate fi atacată. Ministrul Justiţiei, Radu Marinescu, a transmis că „nu poate fi plagiat conţinutul unor legi sau hotărâri judecătoreşti, folosirea terminologiei de specialitate unice, a noţiunilor şi definiţiilor de specialitate curente”. Comisia de Etică a Universităţii din Craiova a publicat, vineri, raportul cu privire la suspiciunea de plagiat, invocată în două sesizări care au vizat lucrarea „Sistemul mijloacelor de probă în procesul civil” (2009), elaborată de Radu Marinescu, scrie News.ro. În 26 de pagini, Comisia prezintă acuzaţiile, demersurile realizate, analiza efectuată de mai mulţi specialişti, dar şi concluziile. Documentul poate fi consultat integral aici (format .pdf, se deschide în pagină separată). „În ceea ce priveşte suspiciunea de plagiat, invocată în cele două sesizări, conform punctelor de vedere transmise de doi specialişti, propuşi de Comisia de Etică Universitară, respectiv conform raportului obţinut cu programul iThenticate (Turnitin), s-a constatat existenţa acestuia. Pe de altă parte, în punctele de vedere transmise de alţi şase specialişti, propuşi de Apărare, s-a afirmat şi s-a argumentat că acuzaţia de plagiat este nefondată. Ca urmare, analiza Comisiei de Etică Universitară, referitoare la existenţa plagiatului sesizat, s-a finalizat cu rezultate caracterizate printr-o profundă ambiguitate epistemologică, concluzia finală plasându-se astfel într-o stare de nedeterminare juridică”, se arată în raport. La final, raportul prezintă decizia Comisiei. „Comisia de Etică Universitară a Universităţii din Craiova hotărăşte: Respinge sesizările nr. 56/13.01.2026 şi nr. 76/14.01.2026, deoarece concluziile specialiştilor, referitoare la suspiciunea de plagiat a tezei de doctorat «Sistemul mijloacelor de probă în procesul civil» (2009), elaborată de domnul R. M., sub coordonarea domnului prof. I. D., sunt contradictorii şi interpretabile. De asemenea, Comisia de Etică Universitară dispune finalizarea analizei dosarului nr. 1/2026”, se mai arată în raport. Concluziile acestuia pot fi contestate, la Comisia Naţională de Atestare a Titlurilor, Diplomelor şi Certificatelor Universitare în termen de 30 de zile de la comunicare. Radu Marinescu a reacţionat, într-un mesaj pe Facebook. „Comisia de etica a Universităţii din Craiova a respins cele doua sesizari privind plagiatul lucrării mele de doctorat. Ma bucur ca s-a constatat nevinovăţia”, a scris, vineri seară, pe Facebook, ministrul Justiţiei, Radu Marinescu. Potrivit acestuia, nu poate fi plagiat conţinutul unor legi sau hotărâri judecătoreşti, folosirea terminologiei de specialitate unice, a noţiunilor şi definiţiilor de specialitate curente. „Chiar dacă softul anti plagiat le detectează automat ca texte copiate, ele sunt, de fapt, conţinut unic, imutabil ştiinţific, doar nu puteai modifica textele de lege. Am sesizat comisiei existenta unui conflict de interese la cei doi experţi auto-propuşi, mai ales că, recent, în cadrul conducerii PSD am respins propunerea USR pentru ca soţia unuia dintre ei să fie numită într-o funcţie înaltă în stat”, a mai transmis ministrul Justiţiei. „Mă bucur că situaţia s-a clarificat şi înţeleg că asta e politică şi că oamenii politici sunt expuşi şi unor asemenea atacuri gratuite, chiar şi după 20 de ani de când o comisie şi toate instituţiile competenţe au evaluat ştiinţific lucrarea şi au decis acordarea titlului de doctor”, a adăugat Marinescu. În 12 ianuarie, PressOne relata că mai mult de jumătate din teza de doctorat în Drept a ministrului Justiţiei, Radu Marinescu, este plagiată. Potrivit analizei PressOne, cel puţin 56,68% dintre paginile lucrării cu titlul „Sistemul mijloacelor de probă în procesul civil” conţin text copiat din alţi autori. Este vorba despre 140 de pagini din cele 247 ale lucrării. Radu Marinescu a obţinut titlul de doctor în Drept în 2009, la Facultatea de Drept şi Ştiinţe Administrative din cadrul Universităţii din Craiova, sub coordonarea profesorului Ion Dogaru.
